competency: IT Project Management Fundamentals :: Functional Analysis

items.stem: A finance lead writes: 'The system shall lock a user account after five failed login attempts.' Which classification is correct, and on what basis?

options.text: Functional, since it names a function the system must execute, which is the axis the classification actually turns on.
options.why: Functional requirements describe the functions the software is to execute, while non-functional ones act to constrain the solution, so a stated behaviour lands on the functional side.

options.text: Non-functional — the five-attempt count is a numeric bound, and a requirement carrying a number constrains quality rather than behaviour.
options.why: The count of failed attempts is part of the function being specified; a non-functional requirement bounds how well a function performs, such as its speed or availability, and numbers appear in both kinds.

options.text: A design decision, since account lockout is an implementation detail better captured as a use case's exception flow.
options.why: Lockout after failed attempts is the behaviour itself, not a mechanism for achieving some other behaviour; it belongs in the requirement, whether or not a use case later elaborates it.

options.text: Non-functional, since account lockout is a security matter and security requirements are always non-functional.
options.why: Security does appear in the standard list of non-functional categories, but that list covers quality constraints; a security behaviour the system must execute, such as locking an account, is a function like any other.

items.rationale: Functional requirements describe the functions the software is to execute; non-functional requirements act to constrain the solution — how well those functions are performed. A number settles nothing on its own: a count of failed attempts is part of the behaviour, while a latency bound is a quality constraint. Neither the subject matter (security, in this case) nor the importance decides the classification.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored, rewritten, re-checked. The original key and o2 turned on 'no threshold attached', which is false on its own stem: 'five failed login attempts' is a numeric threshold, so the item taught that any number pushes a requirement to the non-functional side. SWEBOK v3.0 s1.3 states functional requirements 'describe the functions that the software is to execute' and non-functional ones 'act to constrain the solution'; NASA SEH s4.2.1.2.2 splits functional (what functions are performed) from performance (how well they are performed). Key rewritten to that axis; o2 rewritten to carry the numbers-mean-non-functional misconception explicitly and is false against both sources. o3 (design decision / use-case exception flow) is false: lockout is the behaviour itself. o4 is false because SWEBOK lists security among non-functional categories only as a class of quality constraints, while a security behaviour the system executes is a function; its why was corrected to say so.

items.stem: A requirements document contains: 'The system shall store customer records in PostgreSQL.' Which statement about this sentence is correct?

options.text: It states an implementation choice rather than the need behind it, so it has to be rewritten as behaviour or kept as a constraint with its reason recorded.
options.why: Naming a technology removes a choice the designer has not yet had a chance to make, so the sentence belongs either as the storage and retrieval behaviour it stands in for, or as an explicit design constraint whose rationale is captured with it.

options.text: It is defective in the same way 'the system shall provide flexible reporting' is defective, since neither sentence can be tested as it is written.
options.why: Untestable wording and a smuggled-in solution are different defects; this sentence is perfectly testable and specific, and its problem is that it names a product instead of a need.

options.text: It is a non-functional requirement of the same kind as a stated latency threshold, since both put a measurable bound on how well the system performs.
options.why: A quality requirement has to be quantified to be verifiable, and naming a database product states no measurable level of anything, so it is not a statement of that kind.

options.text: It is a requirement like any other, since every sentence in a requirements document is by definition a requirement.
options.why: Requirements documents routinely carry constraints, assumptions and rationale written in requirement voice; what a sentence is depends on what it states, not on where it happens to sit.

items.rationale: A functional requirement states what the system must do, phrased as an observable outcome rather than an implementation. Naming a vendor, product or protocol is the clearest tell that a solution has been written into requirement voice. The fix is to rewrite it as the behaviour the product was meant to deliver — or, where the choice really is imposed, to keep it as a design constraint and record why the solution was limited to that one method.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored, rewritten, re-checked. The original key asserted the sentence 'is not itself a requirement'. SWEBOK v3.0 s1.2 defines a product requirement as 'a need or constraint on the software to be developed' and s1.3 says non-functional requirements 'act to constrain the solution' — so a mandated product is a constraint that can legitimately sit in the document, which made the original key wrong and the original o3 (non-functional because it bounds the solution) defensible: two answers. NASA SEH s4.2.1 settles the real lesson: 'If the requirement states a method of implementation, the rationale should state why the decision was made to limit the solution to this one method.' Key rewritten to that. o3 rewritten to claim a measurable bound, which is false — SWEBOK s1.5 requires quality requirements to be quantified. o2 is false because the sentence is testable and specific, unlike 'flexible reporting'. o4 is false: the label follows what a sentence states, not where it sits.

items.stem: A backlog review drops a requirement tagged 'non-functional,' reasoning that non-functional items rank below functional ones. What is wrong with that reasoning?

options.text: Classification and priority are independent axes; a non-functional requirement can be the highest-priority item in the set.
options.why: The word 'non-functional' describes what kind of requirement it is, never how important it is — treating it as a synonym for low priority is the single most common inversion.

options.text: The requirement should have been marked 'Won't have' under MoSCoW before being dropped, rather than dropped on classification alone.
options.why: This treats the symptom rather than the mistake: swapping in the right label for 'dropped' still leaves classification standing in for a priority judgement it cannot make.

options.text: The requirement was probably untestable as worded, which is the real defect being missed here.
options.why: Nothing in the scenario suggests the wording is unmeasurable; the stated reasoning is about priority, not testability.

options.text: Nothing is wrong — 'non-functional' is the conventional label for a lower-priority requirement.
options.why: This is the inversion itself, restated as if it were the rule: non-functional requirements are frequently the ones that decide the architecture.

items.rationale: Non-functional requirements constrain how well a behaviour performs, and that classification says nothing about necessity. A team that conflates the two can drop a requirement — often the one deciding the architecture — on no stronger basis than its label.

verification.reasoning: Waived concept, but the point is settleable and consensus. SWEBOK v3.0 s4.1 lists requirements classification dimensions and treats 'whether the requirement is functional or nonfunctional' and 'the requirement priority' as separate dimensions; s1.1 records priority as an attribute carried alongside a requirement. So the key's claim that classification and priority are independent axes is directly supported, and o4 (non-functional as the conventional label for lower priority) is false. o2 is false because relabelling as Won't-have still lets classification stand in for a priority judgement. o3 is false: nothing in the stem concerns testability. No distractor is defensible as an answer to what is wrong with the reasoning given. Sourcing resolved 2026-08-19: the waiver on this concept is lifted. SWEBOK Guide V3.0 Ch.1 s1.3 is now a registered, cited source: "Nonfunctional requirements are the ones that act to constrain the solution. Nonfunctional requirements are sometimes known as constraints or quality requirements."

items.stem: Which of these is a well-formed non-functional requirement?

options.text: 95% of search requests shall complete within 300 ms under normal load.
options.why: It names an attribute, a threshold and the condition it is measured under — the three parts that make a quality requirement measurable rather than aspirational.

options.text: The system shall let a user search by keyword, with no bound on how quickly results return.
options.why: This states a behaviour with no threshold at all, which is what makes it functional rather than non-functional.

options.text: Search performance is listed as a Must have on the delivery backlog.
options.why: This states a priority, not a quality target; a MoSCoW label carries no attribute, threshold or condition to measure against.

options.text: The search feature must be fast and pleasant for users to work with.
options.why: This reads like a quality requirement but has no threshold, so nothing about it can pass or fail — untestable as worded.

items.rationale: A usable non-functional requirement carries an attribute, a metric, a threshold, and the conditions the threshold is measured under. Sentences that state a behaviour without a bound, a priority label, or an unmeasurable adjective all fail one of those parts.

verification.reasoning: Waived concept; the point is a consensus definition and is settleable. SWEBOK v3.0 s1.5 requires requirements to be stated quantitatively where appropriate and names 'the software shall be user-friendly' as the failure mode, which is exactly o4's defect. NASA SEH s4.2.1.2.2 states expected performance 'is expressed as a quantitative measure to indicate how well each product function needs to be accomplished', and Appendix C's verifiability checklist asks whether requirements are free of terms such as flexible, fast and easy. The key carries attribute, threshold and measurement condition, so it is the only well-formed quality requirement. o2 states behaviour with no bound (functional), o3 is a MoSCoW priority label carrying no measurable attribute, o4 is unmeasurable adjectives. No distractor is also correct. Sourcing resolved 2026-08-19: the waiver on this concept is lifted and SWEBOK Guide V3.0, already relied on in this reasoning, is now a registered and directly cited source.

items.stem: Why does practice favor 'requirements elicitation' over 'requirements gathering' as the name for this activity?

options.text: 'Gathering' implies finished requirements already exist and only need collecting; elicitation exists because stated wants and actual needs routinely differ.
options.why: Users describe solutions they have imagined and workarounds become invisible to the people performing them, so the requirements have to be drawn out rather than transcribed.

options.text: Because gathering only covers workflow diagrams, while elicitation also covers written documents.
options.why: Diagramming a workflow is a distinct technique with its own artifact; elicitation is not defined by which artifact it produces.

options.text: Because elicitation identifies the gap between current and desired capability, which gathering cannot do, since gathering only records what stakeholders have already written down.
options.why: Naming that gap is a separate, later technique; elicitation is about drawing needs out of people, not comparing two already-described states.

options.text: There is no real difference between the two terms; they are used interchangeably across most practice guides and style references.
options.why: The word choice is deliberate: 'gathering' presumes the requirements are already there to be picked up, which is exactly the assumption elicitation exists to reject.

items.rationale: Elicitation is the work of drawing requirements out of people — interviews, workshops, observation, document study — rather than collecting requirements that already exist in finished form. A team that only transcribes what it was asked for can build exactly that and still fail the people who asked.

verification.reasoning: Waived concept, but SWEBOK v3.0 settles it directly. s3.2: 'requirements are seldom elicited ready-made. Rather, the software engineer elicits information from which he or she formulates requirements'; 'elicitation is not a passive activity and ... the software engineer has to work hard to elicit the right information. Many business or technical requirements are tacit'; observational techniques are listed precisely because 'many user tasks and business processes are too subtle and complex for their actors to describe easily'. That is the key, including the workarounds-invisible-to-their-performers claim. o4 is therefore false. o2 is false: SWEBOK lists interviews, facilitated meetings, observation, user stories and prototyping, so elicitation is not defined by a diagram artifact. o3 is false: comparing a current to a desired state is gap analysis, a separate technique operating on states already described. Sourcing resolved 2026-08-19: the waiver on this concept is lifted. SWEBOK Guide V3.0 is freely published and is now cited directly (Ch.1 s3.2).

items.stem: A backlog item reads: 'As a claims assessor, I want to flag a suspicious claim, so that it gets reviewed before payment.' A stakeholder calls this a use case. What would need to be added for that to be accurate?

options.text: The actor, preconditions, a numbered main success scenario, and the alternate and exception flows — a use case is written to be complete in itself.
options.why: This sentence is deliberately a placeholder for a conversation still to be had; a use case is meant to be sufficient to build and test from without one.

options.text: Nothing — this is already a complete use case, merely written in a shorter, more casual form for the backlog.
options.why: This is a user story, not a shortened use case; the two differ in intended completeness, not in word count.

options.text: A swimlane diagram showing which department reviews the flagged claim before payment is issued, since that is the artifact that would make the missing detail visible.
options.why: That is process mapping's artifact, for the surrounding business workflow — a use case describes one actor's interaction with the system, not the department hand-offs around it.

options.text: A MoSCoW priority tag showing how urgent the flag is relative to other backlog items.
options.why: Priority is a separate axis from completeness and does not add any of the detail a use case needs.

items.rationale: A use case is written to be sufficient on its own — actor, goal, preconditions, main flow, alternate and exception flows, postcondition. A user story is written to be insufficient on purpose, a reminder that a need must still be discussed. The separating axis is intended completeness, not length.

verification.reasoning: Checked against the cited OMG UML 2.5.1 PDF, text extracted locally (clause 18, p.639 of the spec): a UseCase's behaviours 'can be described by a set of Behaviors ... as well as by pre-conditions, post-conditions and natural language text', and 'A UseCase can include possible variations of its basic behavior, including exceptional behavior and error handling'; UseCases have associated Actors. That supports every element the key names except the numbering of the main success scenario, which is template convention rather than a spec requirement and is not what the item turns on. SWEBOK v3.0 s3.2 describes a user story as containing 'just enough information so that the developers can produce a reasonable estimate', which is the intended-incompleteness contrast, so o2 is false. o3 (swimlane) and o4 (MoSCoW tag) name artifacts that add none of the missing interaction detail. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A use case diagram for a billing system shows an oval labeled 'Generate month-end invoices' connected to an actor labeled 'Scheduler.' A reviewer objects that an automated trigger cannot be an actor. Is the objection correct?

options.text: No. An actor is anything outside the system boundary that initiates or participates in the interaction, human or not.
options.why: A scheduled trigger, or another system, qualifies as an actor for the same reason a person in a role does: it sits outside the boundary and starts the interaction.

options.text: Yes — only a person in a role can be an actor, which is the reason the term is used at all.
options.why: 'Actor' is preferred over 'user' precisely because it is not limited to people; ruling out a scheduled job or an upstream system is wrong on its face.

options.text: The objection is right in spirit — the scheduled trigger should be recorded during elicitation instead of modeled as an actor.
options.why: Elicitation is a separate activity for drawing needs out of people; it does not determine what may appear as an actor in a use case.

options.text: No, but only because the diagram should have been a swimlane process map instead.
options.why: A swimlane map is a different artifact for the surrounding workflow; it is not what settles whether a scheduler can be an actor.

items.rationale: An actor is anyone or anything outside the system boundary that initiates or participates in the interaction — a person in a role, another system, or a scheduled trigger. The diagram itself carries essentially none of the interaction detail; that lives in the use case's flows.

verification.reasoning: Settled verbatim by the cited source. OMG UML 2.5.1 clause 18: 'An Actor models a type of role played by an entity that interacts with the subjects of its associated UseCases ... Actors may represent roles played by human users, external hardware, or other systems', with the note that an Actor is a role of some entity external to the subject. The key is correct and o2 (only a person in a role) is false against that sentence. o3 is false: elicitation is a separate activity and does not govern what may be modelled as an actor. o4 is false: a swimlane map is a different artifact and does not settle the actor question. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A team draws only a to-be swimlane diagram for a redesigned claims workflow and presents it as proof of improvement. What is missing?

options.text: The as-is map; without a baseline of the current workflow there is nothing to demonstrate the difference against.
options.why: A single map of the intended future proves nothing on its own; process maps are usually drawn in two versions precisely so improvement is arguable rather than asserted.

options.text: A gap analysis, since only that technique can say whether the current state is worth changing enough to justify replacing it with the redesigned workflow.
options.why: A gap analysis needs both states already mapped as its input; it does not substitute for drawing the missing as-is map itself.

options.text: A use case for every actor who touches the process.
options.why: A use case documents one actor's interaction with the system; the workflow spans steps no software touches at all, which a use case would not capture.

options.text: Nothing — a single map of the intended future is sufficient once stakeholders agree it looks right.
options.why: Agreement about how the future should look is not the same as showing what changed; without the present-state map there is no baseline to compare against.

items.rationale: Process maps cover the whole workflow, including approvals given verbally and work queued in an inbox. Drawn in pairs — current and intended — they make improvement arguable; the as-is half is also where the unwelcome findings usually live.

verification.reasoning: Cited source checked directly (BPMN 2.0.2 PDF, text extracted locally). Clause 2's list of business processes that can be modelled with BPMN names 'As-is or old Business Process' and 'To-be or new Business Process' as separate model types, and the spec's Relationship example documents 'An as-is and to-be relationship' with type 'reengineered' linking the two models — so the paired current/intended model is a first-class notion in the cited spec, not an invention of the item. The key follows: with only the to-be model there is no baseline the improvement can be shown against. o2 is false because a gap analysis takes both states as input rather than substituting for the missing map. o3 is false: a use case covers one actor's interaction with the system, while the workflow spans steps no software touches. o4 restates the error. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A gap analysis lists six differences between a department's current and desired capability. What can the analysis, by itself, not tell the team?

options.text: Whether closing the gaps is achievable and worth committing to, a judgement that belongs to a feasibility study.
options.why: Gap analysis names the distance between two states; it delivers no judgement about whether closing that distance is achievable, affordable or worth doing.

options.text: How large the differences are between the current and desired states.
options.why: That is exactly what the gap analysis already produced — the six listed differences are its output, not something missing from it.

options.text: What work would be needed to close each of the six differences, since the comparison stops at naming them and leaves the closing actions to a later technique.
options.why: Defining the work that closes the difference is part of the gap analysis itself, not something withheld from it; the six differences and the actions they imply are both its output.

options.text: Nothing — a gap analysis inherently ranks each gap by cost and risk as part of the comparison.
options.why: The comparison is done dimension by dimension to state what is missing, not to rank it; ranking and achievability are both judgements the technique deliberately withholds.

items.rationale: A gap analysis is a structured comparison whose output is the set of differences and the work needed to close them. What it does not deliver is a judgement on achievability, cost or worth — that is a feasibility question, kept deliberately separate.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored for a double key, rewritten, re-checked. The stem asks what the analysis cannot tell, and the original o3 opened 'Which of the six differences should be addressed first' — which the analysis genuinely cannot tell, so the option's leading clause was a second correct answer and only its trailing justification was false. Any option naming something outside gap analysis has that flaw, so o3 was rewritten to name something inside it: the work that closes each difference, which data/topics/06-it-project-management.json defines as part of gap analysis ('Comparing current state to desired state and defining the work that closes the difference') and which the item's own rationale repeats. o3 is now unambiguously false, as are o2 (the sizes are its output) and o4 (it does not rank by cost and risk). The key is correct: achievability and worth are the feasibility question, matching the feasibility-study concept description in the same data file. Waived concept; consensus definition only.

items.stem: A team already has a gap analysis showing six differences between current and desired capability. What question does a feasibility study add that the gap analysis did not answer?

options.text: Whether closing those gaps is technically, operationally and economically achievable, before anyone commits.
options.why: A feasibility study assesses achievability across those dimensions ahead of commitment, which is a different question from naming how far apart two states are.

options.text: How large the differences are between the current and desired states.
options.why: That is exactly what the gap analysis already produced; it is not the question a feasibility study adds.

options.text: Which of the six differences should be addressed first, since ordering by value is treated as part of naming the gaps rather than a separate step.
options.why: Ordering by value is prioritization's job, a separate step from asking whether the work is achievable at all.

options.text: Nothing new — a feasibility study and a gap analysis answer the same question in different words.
options.why: A gap analysis says how far apart the current and desired states are; a feasibility study asks whether closing that distance is achievable and worth committing to at all.

items.rationale: A feasibility study assesses, before commitment, whether a proposal is technically, operationally and economically achievable — with legal and schedule feasibility often added. Recognition of the term and its dimensions is what this level of the exam expects.

verification.reasoning: Waived concept; the item turns on the term's standard dimensions only, which is what the waiver policy permits. SWEBOK v3.0 s2.1 places feasibility studies among the activities that provide input into the requirements process, i.e. before commitment, which is consistent with the key. Checked for a second defensible answer: unlike the paired gap-analysis item, every distractor here is false on its leading clause too — o2 names the gap analysis's own output, o3 names prioritization rather than anything a feasibility study adds, and o4 denies a difference the two concept descriptions state. Recognition-level item; no distractor is also correct. Sourcing resolved 2026-08-19: the waiver on this concept is lifted. SWEBOK Guide V3.0 Ch.7 s1.2 (Feasibility Analysis) is now a registered, cited source and carries the key's three dimensions plus its before-commitment placement: "The purpose of feasibility analysis is to develop a clear description of project objectives and evaluate alternative approaches in order to determine whether the proposed project is the best alternative given the constraints of technology, resources, finances, and social/political considerations." It sits in Ch.7 s1, Initiation and Scope Definition, ahead of Software Project Planning.

items.stem: A backlog owner marks every requirement 'Must have' under MoSCoW, reasoning that each one genuinely matters to the business. What has this prioritization actually achieved?

options.text: Nothing. A scheme where every item is Must has simply relabeled the whole list without forcing any trade-off.
options.why: Prioritization only does work when it forces a choice about what gets dropped under pressure; a list that is entirely Must-have has ordered nothing.

options.text: It has established which gaps between current and desired state are most urgent.
options.why: Naming gaps between two states is gap analysis's output; labeling a backlog with MoSCoW does not perform that comparison.

options.text: It has confirmed that the non-functional requirements are the highest priority.
options.why: Nothing in the scenario distinguishes functional from non-functional; classification and priority are independent axes, and this labeling touches neither.

options.text: It has correctly captured the business's needs, since a Must-have list should include everything that matters.
options.why: This treats prioritization as a record of importance rather than a forced trade-off, which is the failure mode the scenario illustrates.

items.rationale: Prioritization schemes are applied with a cap on the top band or forced ranking precisely because an unconstrained list tends to fill up with Must-haves. The value shows up only at the moment of pressure, converting a shortfall into a planned reduction of scope rather than an argument.

verification.reasoning: Checked against the cited Agile Business Consortium page. Must Haves 'provide the Minimum Usable SubseT (MUST) of requirements which the project guarantees to deliver' — a subset by construction — and DSDM recommends 'typically no more than 60% Must Have effort', stating that 'the safe percentage of Must Have requirements, in order to be confident of project success, is not to exceed 60% Must Have effort', with roughly 20% Could Have contingency. An all-Must backlog therefore leaves no contingency and no trade-off, which is the key, and makes o4 false. o2 is false because MoSCoW labelling performs no current-versus-desired comparison. o3 is false: the scenario does not distinguish functional from non-functional at all. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A traceability matrix shows every numbered requirement linked to at least one test case. What does that demonstrate, and what does it not?

options.text: It demonstrates coverage — every requirement has at least one test linked to it — but not that any test was run or passed, or that the requirement was the right one.
options.why: Traceability shows that a link exists in both directions, forward to tests and back to the need that justified the requirement; it makes no claim at all about outcomes.

options.text: It demonstrates that the system was validated against the real need it was meant to serve, since every requirement has a test exercising it.
options.why: A link between a requirement and a test says nothing about whether the requirement itself was the right one to have — that is a validation question the matrix does not answer.

options.text: It demonstrates that user acceptance testing has been completed for every requirement in the release, since a linked test is an executed test.
options.why: The matrix records links between requirements and tests, not who executed a test or with what outcome.

options.text: It demonstrates that every requirement passed its test, since each one is linked to a test case and none is left uncovered in the matrix.
options.why: A link shows a test exists for the requirement, not that the test was run or that it passed; coverage and correctness are different claims.

items.rationale: Traceability links each requirement forward to design, implementation and test, and back to the need that justified it, so coverage and impact can both be demonstrated. It is confused with testing itself, but a link is not a verdict.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on a narrow point, corrected, re-checked. The original key claimed the matrix showed 'a design and test link', but the stem establishes only test links, so the key asserted evidence the scenario did not contain; it now reads 'at least one test linked to it'. The cited NASA source supports the substance: requirements management maintains 'bidirectional traceability between stakeholder expectations, customer requirements, technical product requirements, product component requirements, design documents, and test plans and procedures', and defines traceability as 'a discernible association between two or more logical entities' — an association, never an outcome. o2 is false (a link is not validation of the need), o3 is false (the matrix records links, not who ran a test), o4 is false (a link is not a pass). No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A release passes 100% of its planned tests, and the traceability matrix shows every requirement covered. Two weeks after go-live, the department is still using its old spreadsheet instead. What does this show?

options.text: Verification succeeded — the system conforms to its specification — but validation was never done, so a wrong specification went undetected.
options.why: A system can pass verification completely and still fail, because conformance to a specification that captured the wrong need is conformance to the wrong thing.

options.text: The traceability matrix must be wrong, since full coverage should have caught the department's non-adoption.
options.why: Coverage is not correctness; the matrix did its job by showing every requirement had a test, and that says nothing about whether the requirement was the right one.

options.text: User acceptance testing must not have been run, since UAT alone verifies conformance to the specification.
options.why: UAT checks the real need, not conformance to the specification — that is what makes it a validation activity, the opposite of the gap this scenario is illustrating.

options.text: Nothing is wrong — passing every test in the plan is itself evidence the project succeeded.
options.why: Passing every test in the plan is evidence of conformance to the specification alone; it is not by itself evidence that the project met the actual need.

items.rationale: Verification asks whether the system was built right, against the agreed specification; validation asks whether the right thing was built, against the actual need. The two checks cannot substitute for each other, which is exactly what a fully-tested, unused system demonstrates.

verification.reasoning: Settled by the cited NASA handbook, read on nasa.gov (section 5.4): 'While verification proves whether the product was done right, validation proves whether the right product was done ... verification provides objective evidence that every shall statement in the requirements document or specification was met, whereas validation is performed for the benefit of the customers and users to ensure that the system functions in the expected manner when placed in the intended environment.' A fully verified, unused system is exactly that gap, so the key holds. o2 is false: coverage is not correctness. o3 is false and inverted — ISTQB CTFL v4.0.1 s2.2.1 states acceptance testing 'focuses on validation', not on conformance to the specification, which is what the option's why already says. o4 is false. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A test team already ran system testing against the specification. During UAT, the same testers re-run the identical scripts at the users' own desks. What has been wasted?

options.text: The one check meant to catch a wrong specification — real users exercising their own work instead of re-verifying conformance.
options.why: UAT is the clearest instance of validation in a delivery; using its slot to repeat verification wastes the only check qualified to catch a wrong specification.

options.text: The specification's traceability, since re-running scripts breaks the link between requirement and test.
options.why: Traceability links persist regardless of who executes a test or how many times; nothing about repeating scripts breaks that link.

options.text: Nothing measurable — repeating verification twice is simply extra assurance, not a waste.
options.why: Extra verification uses up the time and attention meant for validation, which is exactly the resource this scenario shows being spent on the wrong check.

options.text: Nothing — UAT is meant to be a second pass confirming the test team's results.
options.why: Treating UAT as a second pass over the test team's script is the wrong mental model; it should exercise the users' own work against their real needs, not the specification a second time.

items.rationale: UAT is performed by the people who will use the system, against their real work and acceptance criteria, and typically ends in an explicit business sign-off. Run as a repeat of system testing, it stops being a validation activity and becomes a second, redundant verification pass.

verification.reasoning: The cited istqb-standard-glossary-v2.2 URL could not be verified: glossary.istqb.org serves a JavaScript application and returns no term text to a fetch, so the quotation recorded in data/sources.json is not checkable by fetching (reported to the controller, not silently accepted). The claim was settled instead against the ISTQB CTFL v4.0.1 syllabus, s2.2.1: 'Acceptance testing focuses on validation and on demonstrating readiness for deployment, which means that the system fulfills the user's business needs. Ideally, acceptance testing should be performed by the intended users', with UAT named as its main form. That confirms the key: re-running system-test scripts spends the validation slot on verification. o2 is false — traceability links survive re-execution. o3 is false because the repeated verification consumes the time meant for validation. o4 is false against the same sentence. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A specification statement reads: 'The system shall provide flexible reporting and support various export formats.' Why can no test settle whether the delivered system meets it?

options.text: It is ambiguous and unverifiable as written: 'flexible' has no measurable meaning, and it bundles two requirements into a single statement.
options.why: Two readers can hold opposite readings of 'flexible' and both be right, and stating two requirements in one sentence means half of it can pass while the other half fails unnoticed.

options.text: The sentence is fine; 'flexible' is a legitimate non-functional attribute in the same family as availability or performance.
options.why: A real quality attribute needs a threshold and a condition to be measured under; 'flexible' names no measurable quality at all.

options.text: The sentence cannot be traced to a test case, which is the only defect present.
options.why: Traceability is a separate property from testability; an untestable requirement is defective whether or not it happens to be linked to a test case.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it — any sentence phrased as a 'shall' statement is testable by virtue of that phrasing.
options.why: The 'shall' form signals intent to state a requirement, but it guarantees nothing about whether the requirement is measurable.

items.rationale: A specification's quality caps what verification can catch: no test can pass or fail a statement whose terms have no measurable meaning, because no two readers have to agree on what it demands. Review checklists exist to catch exactly this before it reaches a tester — they call out unverifiable words such as 'flexible,' 'user-friendly' and 'fast,' and they require one thought per requirement statement.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED as authored on its premise, rewritten, re-checked. The stem asserted that a reviewer 'cannot fail it in review', which contradicts the cited source: NASA SEH Appendix C's requirements validation checklist exists so that a reviewer can and should fail exactly this sentence — it asks whether requirements are 'free of unverifiable terms (e.g., flexible, easy, sufficient, safe ... user-friendly ...)' and whether they 'express only one thought per requirement statement'. The stem now asks why no test can settle whether the delivered system meets the statement, which is the true defect, and the rationale no longer claims review is powerless. Key confirmed against that checklist and SWEBOK v3.0 s1.5 on avoiding vague, unverifiable requirements. o2 is false ('flexible' names no measurable attribute), o3 is false (traceability and testability are separate properties), o4 is false (the shall form guarantees nothing about measurability). No distractor is also correct.
